goals: Find and treat missing values, duplicates and outliers
why: "Garbage in, garbage out." Practitioners routinely spend most of a project on data preparation. One leaked column can make a useless model look 99% accurate.
explain: **Missing values**: first ask *why* they are missing. Random gaps can be filled (**imputed**) with the median or most frequent value. Gaps that carry meaning ("no income reported") deserve their own indicator column.
**Duplicates**: the same record entered twice inflates its weight. Use `drop_duplicates()` and check business keys such as customer ID.
**Outliers**: some are errors (age = 250); some are real and important (a fraud transaction). Never delete outliers blindly. Investigate them first.

**Leakage**: a feature that would not be known at prediction time, such as "collections_flag" in a default model or "discharge_date" when predicting length of stay. Leakage gives fantastic test scores and a useless model in production.

example.title: Mean or median? Filling missing incomes
steps: Seven applicants' incomes (₹ lakh): 6, 8, missing, 9, 12, missing, 95 (the 95 is a verified business owner)
Mean of the five known = 130 / 5 = ₹26 lakh; median = ₹9 lakh
Mean fill claims both unknown applicants earn ₹26 lakh, more than four of the five known ones; median fill gives a typical ₹9 lakh
Add income_missing = 1 for the two blank rows (0 otherwise) so the model can learn whether a missing income itself signals risk
Keep the 95: it is an outlier, but a real one
example.result: Median for skewed money columns, plus a missing-flag. One genuine high earner made the mean almost three times the median.

mistakes: Imputing before the train/test split, so test information leaks into training.
Dropping every row with any missing value and losing half the data.
Removing outliers that are the very thing you want to detect.
takeaways: Ask why data is missing before filling it
Investigate outliers; do not auto-delete them
Every feature must be available at prediction time

practice.code:
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
df = pd.DataFrame({"income": [6, 8, np.nan, 9, 12, np.nan, 95]})
print(df.income.mean(), df.income.median())      # 26.0 9.0 (NaNs skipped)
df["income_missing"] = df.income.isna().astype(int)
df["income"] = SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit_transform(df[["income"]]).ravel()
print(df)                                        # blanks → 9.0, flag = 1
# In a real project: fit the imputer on the training split only.

options: Number of missed payments after the loan started
